description: Solo team from Singapore. I am a third-year Mechanical Engineering student at Nanyang Technological University, specialising in robotics and mechatronics. I am building HazeLedger, one consistent fire record for Sumatra, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula that joins NASA's MODIS and VIIRS hotspot archives. Skills: engineering analysis, programming and data visualisation. This is a solo entry, so I am not recruiting members.
summary:
What I developed. HazeLedger is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar for Sumatra, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula, from November 2000 to 14 November 2026.

How it addresses the challenge. MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012) cannot be compared directly: here VIIRS reports about 4.8 times as many fires for the same burning. Stitched together, the two NASA archives make Sumatra appear to burn 2.9 times more after 2012, when its fire activity actually fell by about 40%. HazeLedger harmonises 5.3 million NASA FIRMS detections into a single unit, so the sensor of origin no longer matters. Users choose any of 361 provinces and districts, or draw their own area, pick a date range, and see a calendar by day or month, unusual months, critical burning windows, and how the latest month compares with its historical median. Everything can be downloaded.

Why it is important. The method is tested, not assumed: each overlap year was hidden and rebuilt from MODIS alone, cutting the typical error from 80% to 31%. MODIS retires in 2027. Responders, land managers, scientists and haze regulators need a fire record that outlives its sensors. The record is already useful today: it shows October 2026 at 9.4 times the median October.
details:
What does it do?

HazeLedger is a harmonised burning activity calendar. For any place in the region it shows:

  • A calendar with one row per year and one column per day or month, coloured by the number of fire hotspots, with the count printed in each monthly cell.
  • A switch between raw stitched counts, the harmonised record, MODIS only and VIIRS only, so the user can watch the seam between sensors disappear.
  • The latest month against its historical median, with a plain status such as "Far above normal".
  • Critical burning windows, unusual months, yearly totals with an uncertainty range, and the trend with and without harmonisation.
  • NASA's true-colour satellite image for any day the user clicks, so the smoke can be seen directly.
  • Downloads for the chosen place and date range: daily record (CSV), monthly calendar (CSV) and calendar image (PNG).

The area of interest can be one of 6 regional groupings, 29 provinces and states, 326 districts, a rectangle drawn on the map, or typed latitude and longitude.

How does it work?

  1. Every NASA FIRMS detection is counted on a 0.1° grid, per day and per satellite. Only vegetation fires at nominal or high confidence are kept.
  2. The record is expressed in VIIRS-equivalent detections, because VIIRS is the sensor family that continues after MODIS.
  3. In the 2012 to 2025 overlap, each 0.3° block learns its own ratio of VIIRS to MODIS detections, one for each of four burning intensities, pulled toward the regional ratio where a block has few fires.
  4. Before 20 January 2012, MODIS counts are multiplied by the local factor. From 2012 the record is VIIRS itself: Suomi NPP until its last day, 2 November 2026, then NOAA-20.
  5. 60 model variants were compared by hiding one year at a time. The one with the lowest error on hidden years is used, and its errors become the uncertainty range shown on rebuilt years.

Does it work?

  • Typical monthly error per province on hidden years: 80% if MODIS counts are used as they are, 31% with HazeLedger. Two identical VIIRS instruments 50 minutes apart disagree by 16%, which is the floor no method can beat.
  • Annual totals per province: typical error 12%. Agreement on a log scale: R² 0.83 over 3,546 province-months.
  • Across the 2012 join, Sumatra's harmonised average year changes 0.62 times, in step with MODIS alone (0.60 times). Raw stitched counts claim 2.9 times.
  • Independent check: monthly Singapore PSI and the harmonised Sumatra fire count have a rank correlation of 0.67 over 150 months.

What benefits does it have?

  • Early warning and emergency responders can see at once whether this month is above normal for a district and whether it is inside its critical burning window.
  • Land managers and scientists get a consistent 26 year series for any area, with uncertainty, as CSV.
  • Regulators and lenders get a baseline that does not jump when a satellite changes, which Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act and sustainable finance rules both need.

What is the intended impact?

A fire record that survives its satellites. MODIS retires in 2027 and Suomi NPP stopped delivering in November 2026. The same method carries the record on to NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, and extending it to another region means changing a list of countries and a bounding box. The public calendar is free. A sustainable version would fund itself through an API and area reports for organisations that must document fire history, such as commodity buyers and banks.

How is it creative?

  • It converts the old record up to VIIRS units, the units of the future, instead of degrading VIIRS down to MODIS.
  • The correction is not one number. It depends on place and on how intensely the surroundings are burning: VIIRS sees 6.8 times as many fires as MODIS where burning is scattered, and about 4 times where it is heavy.
  • It uses two identical VIIRS instruments to measure the lowest error any method could reach, and reports its own error against that floor.
  • It checks itself against something outside fire data: the air Singapore breathed. In 2013, Singapore's worst PM10 year, Sumatra's annual total ranked only 9th of 25, but the calendar shows Riau at about 30 times its median June.
  • The app shows its evidence. The hold-out tests and the model comparison are on the page, not in an appendix.

What factors did I consider?

  • Validity: calibration and all tests use science-quality archive years only. Near-real-time 2026 data is added afterwards and labelled.
  • Honesty about limits: fires too small for MODIS on a given day are restored in totals, not in timing. Cloud and thick smoke hide fires from both sensors. A hotspot is an observation of heat, not proof of who lit a fire. The record shows burning fell after 2015 but cannot say how much is weather and how much is policy.
  • Accessibility: a single-hue colour ramp from light to dark, counts printed in cells, text labels beside every colour status, and a layout that works on a phone.
  • Users with no technical background: plain-language labels and one headline switch.

What tools, coding languages and software did I use?

  • Data pipeline: Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Shapely), run in Google Colab.
  • Web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas and SVG. No framework, no server, no API keys. Hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Code: https://github.com/yihang-ooi/hazeledger

Where and how SI tools were used

The code, the data analysis and the text of this project were produced with Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, under the author's direction. This is stated in the site footer, the repository README, the header of every script and the metadata of the data file. No SI-generated images, video or audio are used: every chart is drawn by code from NASA data, the satellite photos come from NASA GIBS, and the demo video is a screen recording. No NASA branding is used.
